stem: An adult has nasal discharge and congestion that have persisted for 12 days without improvement. Which condition should the nurse recognize as most consistent with this pattern?

options.B: A typical brief viral upper respiratory infection

rationale: CDC outpatient guidance states that acute bacterial rhinosinusitis can be diagnosed when symptoms persist for more than 10 days without improvement, such as ongoing nasal discharge or daytime cough. The 12-day course without improvement therefore supports A. The item intentionally does not combine this persistent-symptom criterion with the separate severe-disease criterion of high fever plus purulent discharge or facial pain.
educational_objective: Recognize persistent sinonasal symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement as a clinical pattern that supports acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in adults.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Outpatient Clinical Care for Adults — Antibiotic Prescribing and Use
source_version_date: Page dated 2024-04-16; current CDC page accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Adult Treatment Recommendations > Acute rhinosinusitis > Diagnosis: diagnose acute bacterial rhinosinusitis when symptoms are severe, persistent (>10 days) without improvement, or worsening after initial improvement; persistent examples include nasal discharge or daytime cough
source_claim_supported: In adults, acute bacterial rhinosinusitis is supported by persistent sinonasal symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, Pathophysiology, printed p.48 / PDF p.51: identify pathophysiology related to an acute or chronic condition; Illness Management: apply knowledge of client pathophysiology to illness management
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — Illness Management / recognition of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis
correction_summary: Separated the CDC persistent-symptom diagnostic criterion from the distinct severe-disease criterion instead of combining duration, facial pain, and purulence into one unsupported rule. Reframed the item around an adult with >10 days of symptoms without improvement and replaced weak distractors with clinically plausible alternatives.
audit_findings: A is directly supported by current CDC adult outpatient guidance. B is less consistent because a typical viral URI is expected to improve rather than remain unimproved beyond the CDC bacterial-rhinosinusitis threshold. C and D do not fit the persistent infectious sinonasal pattern described. The stem does not imply that every sinus infection requires antibiotics, does not use imaging as a diagnostic requirement, and does not conflate the persistent, severe, and worsening diagnostic pathways. No second answer, cueing, or unsupported treatment claim remains. NCSBN 2026 supports the Physiological Adaptation mapping through Pathophysiology and Illness Management.
